description: A shrub of thin, upright stems, or a vine that climbs high up oak trunks, with leaves in threes that are shiny green in spring and turn bright red in fall; 1-3 m tall as a shrub here. It grows everywhere under and around the oaks, and every child in the foothills learns the rhyme 'leaves of three, let it be': its oil gives people an itchy rash, so it is not to be touched, even when the branches are bare, though deer browse it and birds eat its white berries.

season_notes.winter: Bare grey stems with no leaves, and it can still give you a rash, so do not touch any bare stems you are not sure about.
season_notes.spring: New leaves in threes come out shiny and red-tinged in March, then turn bright green; small greenish-white flowers hang in April. Leaves of three, let it be!
season_notes.summer: Glossy green leaves of three; in dry spots some leaves already turn red and drop early. Tiny white berries ripen in hanging bunches.
season_notes.fall: The brightest red in the woodland: whole patches turn scarlet, orange and yellow before the leaves drop in November.

notes: Pacific poison oak is the commonest woody plant of the oak woodland understory in the foothills, from grassland edges to shady canyons, 0.5-4 m as a shrub and up to 20 m or more as a vine up oak trunks (aerial rootlets). Form: plain 'shrub'. A few (3-7) slender, upright to leaning stems from spreading underground runners, little branched, leafy on their upper two thirds: open (porosity 0.35), taller than wide (W/H 0.55-1.0), crown base about 0.15; old colonies make thickets of many stems ('thicket' class) and young plants are a few leafy shoots in the grass ('low' class). Bark smooth grey-brown with small lenticels, twigs red-brown. Leaves alternate, compound with three leaflets 3-10 cm, the end leaflet on a longer stalk, lobed or wavy-edged like a small oak leaf: leaf_shape trifoliate, leaf_size_m 0.1 for the whole leaf of three. Shiny when young. Seasons: leafing in March, red-tinged at first (spring colour bronze), bright to dark green by May, drought-stressed plants redden and drop leaves from late summer, the whole shrub scarlet, orange and yellow in October, bare from November to February (leaf_on_by_month). Flowers small, greenish-white in hanging clusters in April; fruit a hanging cluster of small whitish-tan drupes from late summer. All parts carry urushiol, which causes the rash, in every season including bare winter stems. Not drawn: the vine form on tree trunks (a later lane could add it to the oaks, e.g. as an epiphyte like the mistletoe, or as a trunk texture).
